title: AgenticRag-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Stack Memory for Multi-Step Reasoning, Retrieval and Memorizing

paper.title: AgenticRag - R1 : Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Stack Memory for Multi-Step Reasoning, Retrieval and Memorizing
paper.abstract:
Abstract Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models (LLMs), yet existing RAG systems often struggle with complex, multi-step reasoning that requires adaptive retrieval and continuous revision of intermediate contexts .
Recent reinforcement learning (RL)-based agentic RAG methods partially alleviate this issue, but typically rely on coarse-grained action spaces and trajectory-level rewards , resulting in weak reward assignment and a bias toward short-horizon, stereotyped reasoning template.
To address, we propose AgenticRag -R1, a RL framework that deeply integrates reasoning, retrieval, and memory via a memory stack and fine-grained action space, supported by hierarchical action-aware rewards and an information-aware trajectory rejection strategy to enable effective long-horizon learning.
Experiments across a diverse set of multi-hop, open-domain, and agentic reasoning benchmarks, spanning multiple backbone model sizes, demonstrate that AgenticRag -R1 consistently outperforms strong baselines.
Moreover, AgenticRag -R1 learns more robust, interpretable, and memory-aware reasoning behaviors, highlighting the effect of fine-grained action modeling and information-aware optimization for long-horizon reasoning.
Our code is anonymous available at https://github.com/jiangxinke/Harness-RL/tree/AgenticRAG-R1-Whitebox .

zhaojf, wangyasha}@pku.edu.cn Abstract Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models (LLMs), yet existing RAG systems often struggle with complex, multi-step reasoning that requires adaptive retrieval and continuous revision of intermediate contexts . Recent reinforcement learning (RL)-based agentic RAG methods partially alleviate this issue, but typically rely on coarse-grained action spaces and trajectory-level rewards , resulting in weak reward assignment and a bias toward short-horizon, stereotyped reasoning template. To address, we propose AgenticRag -R1, a RL framework that deeply integrates reasoning, retrieval, and memory via a memory stack and fine-grained action space, supported by hierarchical action-aware rewards and an information-aware trajectory rejection strategy to enable effective long-horizon learning. Experiments across a diverse set of multi-hop, open-domain, and agentic reasoning benchmarks, spanning multiple backbone model sizes, demonstrate that AgenticRag -R1 consistently outperforms strong baselines. Moreover, AgenticRag -R1 learns more robust, interpretable, and memory-aware reasoning behaviors, highlighting the effect of fine-grained action modeling and information-aware optimization for long-horizon reasoning. Our code is anonymous available at https://github.com/jiangxinke/Harness-RL/tree/AgenticRAG-R1-Whitebox . 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a broad range of natural language processing tasks Kaplan et al. (2020) ; Yang et al. (2024b) ; Guo et al. (2025) ; Vu et al. (2024) ; Chang et al. (2024) . However, despite their strengths, LLMs still remain prone to factual errors Ji et al. (2023b) ; Cao et al. (2020) ; Ji et al. (2023a) ; Jiang et al. (2024b) , outdated knowledge He et al. (2022) and limited domain-specific expertise Kandpal et al. (2023) , making R etrieval- A ugmented G eneration (RAG) Edge et al. (2024) ; Asai et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024c) a promising solution by enabling access to external knowledge for improved accuracy and adaptability. Figure 1: Conventional Agentic vs AgenticRag -R1 for multi-step reasoning and retrieval. Conventional methods adopt coarse-grained, append-only memory and shallow retrieval, leading to error accumulation and short-horizon. AgenticRag -R1 employs fine-grained, reversible memory actions and information-aware rollout selection, for robust long-horizon reasoning. In contrast, many real-world decision-making tasks are inherently complicated Gao et al. (2025) , requiring models to decompose problems into multiple interdependent steps rather than relying on one-off reasoning or single-step retrieval Shao et al. (2023) ; Press et al. (2022) . Such settings demand not only access to external knowledge, but also the ability to dynamically decide when and what to retrieve as the reasoning process unfolds Lee et al. (2024) ; Jeong et al. (2024) . Crucially, retrieved information could be continuously integrated into the model’s evolving internal state, influencing subsequent reasoning and decision making. This tight coupling between reasoning and retrieval makes their deep integration a critical yet underexplored challenge. Early attempts to integrate reasoning and retrieval primarily relied on manually crafted prompting strategies Press et al. (2022) ; Shao et al. (2023) ; Trivedi and others (2023) ; Jiang et al. (2024a) ; Li et al. (2025) , and were later extended through S upervised F ine- T uning (SFT) to better coordinate their interaction Wang et al. (2025b) . While effective in specific settings, these approaches depend heavily on heuristic design and often overfit to fixed reasoning patterns , without intrinsically improving the model’s ability to jointly reason and retrieve Chu et al. (2025a) . More recently, R einforcement L earning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning, as demonstrated by OpenAI O1 OpenAI (2025) and DeepSeek-R1 Guo et al. (2025) . Motivated by this success, several studies have begun to apply RL to retrieval-augmented settings, training models to invoke external retrieval tools during reasoning Jin et al. (2025) ; Dong et al. (2025a) ; Dong et al. (2025b) ; Zhou et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2026) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , most existing RL-based RAG rely on coarse-grained action modeling , treating retrieval as a single or shallow action, which limits fine-grained control over complex tasks and biases policy learning toward short-horizon , easily reproducible reasoning templates than long-horizon retrieval and reasoning, posing two challenges: ❶ Challenge 1. How to expose fine-grained, memory-aware action-making and reward allocation in multi-step reasoning and retrieval. Deep integration of reasoning and retrieval requires LLMs not only to acquire external information , but also to continuously manage and revise intermediate content memory under noisy and uncertain conditions. In multi-step reasoning, both external retrieval and internal inference inevitably introduce noise: retrieved documents may be irrelevant or misleading Yao et al. (2022b) ; Shinn et al. (2023) ; Liu et al. (2023) , while intermediate reasoning steps may contain logical errors or overconfident assumptions Jiang et al. (2024a) ; Xiong et al. (2024) ; Hao et al. (2023) . If such noisy intermediate conclusions are written into context memory without the ability to be inspected, revised, or discarded, they tend to propagate and amplify over steps, effectively corrupting the agent’s internal decision state Ning et al. (2025) ; Hoscilowicz et al. (2024) ; Lai et al. (2024) . However, most existing RL-based agentic methods adopt a highly coarse-grained action formulation, collapsing the entire reasoning and retrieval processes into a single latent and memory-appending <think> and <search> action template Dong et al. (2025a) ; Dong et al. (2025b) ; Zhou et al. (2025) , which are then stored as irreversible content. This limitation is further exacerbated by reward design, where outcome rewards are evaluated only on final correctness, overlooking the contributions of intermediate actions throughout the trajectory Shao et al. (2024) ; Jin et al. (2025) . Without fine-grained, memory-aware action and reward signals, RL suffers from weak reward assignment and is biased toward shallow, template-like strategies . ❷ Challenge 2. How to expose reinforcement learning to sufficiently diverse and high-information reasoning and retrieval rollouts. Even with fine-grained action spaces and memory-aware reward mechanisms, RL may still fail to learn robust long-horizon reasoning if the training distribution is dominated by low information trajectories . Most multi-hop and retrieval-augmented tasks are simple—requiring only a single retrieval step or shallow reasoning —so these short-horizon trajectories often yield higher immediate rewards than more complex, long-horizon ones Gao et al. (2025) ; Zhou et al. (2025) . As a result, RL tends to overfit to low-information , trivially rewarding trajectories, rarely exercising actions such as revising, summarizing, or planning, and under-optimizing the long-horizon combinations of cognitive actions Wang et al. (2025c) .
